description: prConcurrentLimit and prHourlyLimit are 0, which is Renovate's spelling of 'no limit'. They are NOT redundant lines to tidy away: deleting them restores the defaults of 10 concurrent and 2 per hour, so the throttle would come back silently.

What replaced them is the dashboard gate — for everything EXCEPT patches, which are exempt from both and never become pull requests at all (see the patch rule below). So patches are the one unbounded category: they land on their own, in whatever quantity a given day produces, each firing the full CI matrix against a renovate/patch-* branch. That is the deliberate shape of this config, not an oversight, but it is the thing to change first if the runners ever suffer for it.
ignorePathsDescription: Generated build output ONLY. `android/**` and `ios/**` used to be listed wholesale, and that removed two of the four shipped platforms from dependency automation entirely: the AGP and google-services pins in android/build.gradle, the eleven androidx/Cordova versions in android/variables.gradle, the Gradle wrapper, and the iOS SPM graph — none of it watched by anything.

The reason that mattered more than a missed minor: ignorePaths is evaluated BEFORE package rules, so the vulnerabilityAlerts block below — the one category deliberately exempt from the dashboard gate — could not reach these files either. An advisory against androidx.webkit, which backs the WebView rendering an E2EE client, produced no branch, no PR and no dashboard row. Silent by construction.

What remains here is the copy of the web build each native shell embeds. Those trees are `pnpm build` output committed into the platform projects; a lockfile or manifest found inside one is a stale artefact, not a dependency, and updating it would be updating a build product.

description: A security fix must never sit behind a tick nobody has looked at, so this opts out of the dashboard gate as well as the three-day soak. It is the one category where a delay is the risk rather than the safeguard.

The last three keys exist because a security fix is frequently ALSO a patch, and would otherwise inherit the patch rule's no-pull-request automerge. Renovate injects each vulnerability as a package rule carrying this object as `force`, which outranks the ordinary rules — but only for the keys it contains, and automerge/automergeType/additionalBranchPrefix are not among them by default. Left inherited, a security patch merges as a bare branch: the `security` label below is never applied (labels are a pull request thing), and the CVE detail Renovate writes into prBodyNotes is discarded with the PR that never existed. The commit says `[SECURITY]` and nothing records WHICH advisory it closed.

So security updates keep a pull request, and it costs no latency: prCreation is `immediate` by default here, and automerge — where the patch rule turned it on — merges the moment CI is green, exactly as it did before patches moved to branches. The empty additionalBranchPrefix also keeps these off renovate/patch-*, which ci.yml treats as 'no PR exists': with both a push trigger and a pull request, the five jobs would run twice.

platformAutomerge is false for the reason it was originally false on the patch rule: GitHub's native auto-merge waits only for checks a branch protection rule marks REQUIRED, and develop has no protection rule, so nothing is required and a red run would not stop the merge. Renovate merging it itself means the branch is verified green first. Not needed on the patch rule any more — branch automerge never involves a pull request for the platform to act on — but very much needed here.

Patch updates are the one category that needs no human at any point: exempt from the dashboard gate, and merged by Renovate once CI is green. A patch is the update type least likely to change behaviour, and minimumReleaseAge already holds every release for three days, so a version yanked hours after publishing never reaches a branch in the first place. Everything else waits for a tick under the top-level dependencyDashboardApproval.

automergeType 'branch' means these never become pull requests: Renovate pushes renovate/*, waits for that branch's checks, and merges it into develop itself. A PR is the fallback rather than the route — Renovate opens one if the branch goes red, or if its checks stay pending for 24 hours — so a failing patch still surfaces somewhere a human can see it, it just arrives as a PR instead of a merge. platformAutomerge is deliberately NOT set here: it only governs GitHub's native auto-merge on a pull request, and there is no pull request in this path.

additionalBranchPrefix puts these on renovate/patch-* instead of renovate/*, and it exists to keep ci.yml's push trigger narrow. CI has to run on the branch for any of this to work (below), but a trigger of renovate/** would also match every dashboard-approved update — which DOES get a pull request — and each rebase there would then fire a push run and a pull_request run of the same five jobs, e2e included. The prefix makes the push trigger match only the branches that never become a PR. Renovate composes branch names as branchPrefix + additionalBranchPrefix + branchTopic from the config resolved for each update, so a rule-level value is applied here and nowhere else.

This rule depends on ci.yml running on push to renovate/patch-**, and the dependency is one-directional and silent. With no checks on the branch Renovate declines to merge (automerging an untested branch needs an explicit ignoreTests, which is not set), so it waits out the pending window and opens a PR. Removing that trigger therefore breaks nothing loudly — it quietly turns this whole rule back into ordinary pull requests.

rebaseWhen is overridden because nothing reads these branches before they land. With no protection rule on develop there is no 'branch must be up to date' gate, so the green result Renovate merges on could otherwise have been produced against a base that has since moved. 'behind-base-branch' re-runs CI against the current base before that can happen. It costs extra CI on branches the base outpaces, which is the right way round for the only rule that merges with nobody looking.

packageRules.description: Angular and everything version-locked to it. These must move together — a partial bump leaves @angular/compiler-cli disagreeing with @angular/core and the build fails outright.
Nx and its plugins are released in lockstep and share a workspace version.
The Rust crypto WASM is coupled to the SDK that loads it; bumping one alone is how the E2EE init breaks.
Capacitor core, CLI and every plugin track one major — including the third-party ones, which peer-depend on @capacitor/core and break if they lag behind it.
Brain (headless) and the CLI that generates the Helm components from it.
The Playwright runner and its browser package must match, or the browsers are re-downloaded and the versions disagree.
Vitest core and its coverage provider.
ESLint and the plugins that peer-depend on it.
Tailwind v4 is CSS-configured; its PostCSS plugin and the prettier plugin follow the same version.

The desktop shell is a separate package with its own lockfile and its own toolchain, so its updates must never be merged into a root group. TypeScript is the one exception, carved back out by the rule immediately below.

description: TypeScript follows Angular, not npm's latest, and electron/ follows the workspace. @angular/compiler-cli peer-depends on a single minor window — `>=6.0 <6.1` on Angular 22 — and pnpm only warns about an unmet peer rather than refusing to install, so a TypeScript minor bumped on its own would install cleanly and then fail in ngtsc, where it reads as an Angular bug rather than a dependency one.

This ceiling has to be widened BY HAND when an Angular major lands, and the Angular group's own PR is the moment to do it: read the new window off `pnpm view @angular/compiler-cli@<version> peerDependencies`. Until then, the Angular PR is what fails, not this one — Angular 23 requiring a TypeScript this rule still forbids shows up as a red Angular PR, not as a silently skipped update.

The desktop shell used to pin its own TypeScript 5.9 against the workspace's 6.x. That divergence was not free: @nx/js ships tsconfig codemods on every root TypeScript bump, they glob electron/tsconfig.json along with everything else, and the rewritten file then failed to parse under the older compiler — a breakage that arrived through a migration nobody ran against electron/, in a package CI builds separately. Both manifests now move as one version, in one branch.

ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: this rule must stay BELOW the electron shell rule. Renovate merges every matching packageRule in array order and the last one wins each key, so electron/'s TypeScript picks up groupName 'typescript' here only because this rule comes second. Move it above and the shell rule silently reclaims it into the 'electron shell' group — two branches, two versions, and the divergence is back with nothing to show it.
rangeStrategy pin keeps both manifests on an exact, textually identical version rather than a caret that could drift apart within the allowed window.

electron/tsconfig.json must stay on `module`/`moduleResolution` Node16 for this to hold. TypeScript 6 rejects the old node10 resolution outright (TS5107), so a revert to `Node` there breaks the desktop build the next time this rule fires.

The native build graphs, now that ignorePaths no longer hides them: Gradle (AGP, google-services, the eleven androidx/Cordova pins Capacitor writes into android/variables.gradle), the Gradle wrapper, and the iOS Swift package at ios/App/CapApp-SPM/Package.swift. No cocoapods rule — this project has no Podfile; Capacitor 8 generates SPM instead.

Grouped into ONE branch because Capacitor pins these versions as a set: androidx.webkit, androidx.core and the Cordova compatibility shims are chosen to match the @capacitor/android that ships them, and moving one of them alone is how you get a resolution conflict that only appears at assemble time.

dependencyDashboardApproval stays true — inherited from the top level and restated here so it survives someone reordering these rules. A native bump cannot be judged by CI: nothing in this repo builds an APK or an .ipa (see ci.yml), so the only real verification is a device or emulator build, which is a human act. That is the reason to gate them, NOT a reason to hide them — the point of narrowing ignorePaths is that vulnerabilityAlerts, which opts out of this gate, can now reach them at all.
Action digests are pinned for supply-chain reasons (see .github/actions/setup/action.yml); this is what keeps the pins from rotting.

It opts back OUT of the patch automerge above, and that is not a stylistic preference. A pinned action reads `owner/action@<sha> # v7.0.1`, so a v7.0.1 to v7.0.2 bump is updateType 'patch' and would otherwise qualify — but unlike a library patch it repoints a SHA at new third-party code that runs inside CI, including release.yml, whose environment holds the signing certificates. Merging that unattended into an unprotected branch is precisely the exposure the digest pinning exists to prevent: retargeting a tag is how CVE-2025-30066 reached ~23k repositories. These stay behind a tick and a human.

Opting out of the automerge means it must also opt out of that rule's branch prefix, hence the empty additionalBranchPrefix — this rule matches patches, so it would otherwise inherit renovate/patch-*, which ci.yml treats as 'no pull request exists for this branch'. An action digest bump is one of the more frequent updates here, so leaving it inherited is a doubled CI run — push and pull_request — on most of them.
